skills.name: Practical preparation: pie charts and totals

note.text: A pie chart divides a whole into sectors. Each sector represents a share of the same total; sector angles add to a full turn. The larger the share, the larger its angle. Calculate a share by dividing the category's value by the total, then multiply by the angle of a full turn. The chart is inappropriate when the categories overlap and cannot form one whole. Keep the total and unit visible.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: A pie chart divides a whole into sectors. Each sector represents a share of the same total; sector angles add to a full turn. The larger the share, the larger its angle. Calculate a share by dividing the category's value by the total, then multiply by the angle of a full turn. The chart is inappropriate when the categories overlap and cannot form one whole. Keep the total and unit visible.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: A classroom record divides a fruit stall's basket sales into oranges, bananas and plantains. These categories form one counted total. The pie chart represents proportions, not the number of traders. A half share occupies half the circle. Before drawing, add all category counts and check that no basket has been counted twice.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Add the values, calculate each fraction and convert it to an angle. Check that the angles sum to {360} degrees. Use a key to identify sectors. Do not use each separate category as its own denominator: every share refers to the common total.

key_words.meaning: a wedge representing part of a whole
the sum of all category values in the chart
a category's value divided by the common total
the share multiplied by the degrees in a full turn
